Reason to be thankful? We had a pre-recorded Facts vs Feelings for this week, but Mr Market had other plans 📉 📈 

Enjoy Ep.215 What The Heck Just Happened 

Stocks just staged a historic rebound after a historic sell-off. @sonusvarghese and I break it down

📉 The S&P 500 fell 11.5% from its October 6 peak, but tech fell about 26% and every other sector held up better. The correction took only 33 trading days, and just 3 of the 10 fastest corrections became bear markets, compared with 6 of the 10 slowest

🏦 The KBE bank index broke out above its 2007 peak and has held there. Credit spreads are tight everywhere outside CCC debt, which ties to the neo-cloud names. The thing to watch is roughly $4.5 trillion in off-balance sheet AI commitments

🔄 From March to December 2000, tech fell 48% while financials gained 23% and healthcare gained 37%. Sonu favors adding healthcare, financials, and energy and keeping tech close to neutral

🦅 Governor Waller wants a 50 bp hike in December. With core PCE at 3.2% and unemployment at 4.1%, Sonu sees little case for a pause and says the policy rate could approach 5%

😱 The VIX spiked to 40, the put/call ratio hit its highest level since Liberation Day, and NAAIM exposure fell to its lowest since April. November through January has historically been the best three-month stretch of the year

Plus what we are grateful for this Thanksgiving 🦃

Full episode 👇

tweets.text:
@C_Barraud's Morning Brief today packed as always and included a Bloomberg story noting the S&P 500 is set to match its choppiest streak since the 2022 bear market with four straight weeks with a move of at least 2.5% in either direction: −2.7%, +2.5%, −8.6% (the worst week since April 2025) and +3.9% so far this week.

Streaks like this look like a bear market thing, so I ran it back to 1928 to see how often they happen outside one.

▪️ There have been 39 prior streaks of four or more straight 2.5%+ weeks. 33 came during bear markets, defined as a 20%+ decline, counted from the prior peak until a new high (the way Bloomberg shades them).
▪️ The six exceptions were August 1929, October 1955, October 1989, September 1997, October 1999 and February 2000. If this week holds, it would be the first four-week streak outside a bear market in nearly 27 years. The S&P would need to fall more than 1.4% in Friday's half session for it not to hold.
▪️ Five weeks is where the line really gets drawn. All 21 streaks that reached five weeks came during bear markets, including all six since 1950 (1962, 1973, 1974, 2008, 2009 and 2022).
▪️ The bear wasn't always obvious at the time, though. When the 1973 streak hit four weeks, the S&P was only 14% off its high. The streak ran to seven weeks, and the decline ended up at 48%.

What came next is mixed. After the six streaks outside a bear, the S&P was higher a month later every time, with a median gain of +3.9%. A year later, though, the median was −1.0%, and only three of six were higher. For all weeks since 1928, the median one-year gain is +9.6%, with 70% higher. Two of those streaks, August 1929 and February 2000, came within about five weeks of major tops. October 1989 came before the 1990 decline that stopped just short of a bear market (−19.9%).

Streaks during bear markets tended to show up nearer the lows. Their median one-year gain was +14.9%, or +17.8% since 1950, with eight of nine higher.

The sample is small, but if history is a guide, next week matters. A fifth straight 2.5%+ week would either be the first outside a bear market in nearly a century of data, or a sign this is more than a correction.

The problem with predicting the bottom is that the price is already up by 25% or more.

Based on my dictionary, the bottom is in place if it gives the following sequence

Low, High, higher low, lower high, and finally a new high.
subtle variation
Low, High, higher low, higher-high

Look at $SOXX chart; the sequence that we got is:
Low, High, higher low, lower high, and then lower-low

We are still in the process of a downtrend
And when you are trading counter-trend, you need to be familiar with the rules of engagement

Overnight risk is real; sizing and cushion help navigate

tweets.text:
Is this a bubble? No… not yet.

Since 1981, the MACROSHARK Bubble Index has only reached bubble territory at the 1987, 2000, 2007 and 2021 peaks. We're not there.

But 2026 moved it fast. In May it was higher than about 60% of all months since 1981. Today it's higher than 88%.

Readings this high haven't meant the top is in. They've meant the odds tilt: lower returns over the following 12 months, and bigger drawdowns along the way.

The rubber band is stretched, not snapped.

Finally, Happy Thanksgiving to everyone who celebrates!

tweets.text:
For those of us left here in crypto, as we wallow in sorrow, there are some interesting analogies to consider about where we are right now and what we're seeing in DeFi from a revenue-generation perspective, not to mention the improving value accrual trend: it is akin to the Nasdaq post the 2001 bubble burst.

If 2021 marked the hype-cycle peak for crypto, which it most certainly was, driven by excess liquidity and a pre-AI world, then DeFi is doing exactly what the Nasdaq did in the years that followed. Adoption is accelerating, revenues are expanding, and multiples are compressing. 

By 2006, the NDX had 2-3x from the lows and its P/E halved. 

In DeFi, revenue is 5.5x, and the multiple is sub-10x (down 80%). At some point, this matters. 

... unless, of course, 2027/2028 turns into a 2007/2008! Not my base case!
